interactions.title: Check yourself: version control, Git and GitHub

topics.after: Git's Role in a Software Team

questions.prompt: Which statement about Git and GitHub is correct?
options: Git needs a GitHub account to work
GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds pull requests, issues and Actions
Pull requests are stored in the Git history
GitLab is an alternative to Git
questions.explanation: Git is the version control tool and works offline; GitHub is a hosting and collaboration platform. GitLab and Bitbucket are alternatives to GitHub, not to Git.

questions.prompt: In a distributed system such as Git, where does the complete history live?
options: Only on the machine of the person who created the repository
questions.explanation: Every clone contains the full history up to its last fetch, so most operations are local and history survives the loss of any one copy.

questions.prompt: Priya committed yesterday but never pushed. Her laptop is stolen. What did the team lose?
questions.explanation: Committing is local. Only pushed commits exist on the shared remote; unpushed commits (and any uncommitted work) were only on her laptop.

questions.prompt: ~/.gitconfig sets user.email = a@example.com and the repository's .git/config sets b@example.com. Which email do new commits in this repository use?
questions.explanation: Local configuration overrides global, which overrides system.

questions.prompt: target/ was committed last week. You add target/ to .gitignore. What happens?
options: Nothing changes for target/ until you run git rm -r --cached target/
questions.explanation: .gitignore only affects untracked files. Untrack with git rm -r --cached, then commit; old commits still contain the files.

questions.prompt: Which rules keep logs/README.md tracked while ignoring everything else in logs/?
questions.explanation: If the directory itself is ignored (logs/), Git never looks inside, so a negation can't re-include a file. Ignore the contents (logs/*) instead.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the exact .gitignore line that ignores a file?
questions.explanation: git check-ignore -v prints the source file, line number and pattern for each ignored path.

questions.prompt: git status -s shows MM App.java. What will git commit record for App.java?
options: Nothing — the file is in conflict
questions.explanation: MM means staged, then modified again. A commit records the index; the newer edit stays unstaged.

questions.prompt: You created Student.java and edited App.java, then ran git commit -am "Add Student". What is committed?
questions.explanation: -a stages modified and deleted tracked files only; the new file remains untracked.

questions.prompt: Which command shows exactly what the next commit will contain?
questions.explanation: git diff compares the working directory with the index (unstaged changes); --staged compares the index with HEAD.

questions.prompt: Which is the best commit subject?
options: Updated GradeCalculator.java and its test file because of the issue
Reject an empty marks list in average()
questions.explanation: Imperative, specific and short; it describes the change, not the files.

questions.prompt: HEAD is a merge commit. Which reference names the tip of the branch that was merged in?
questions.explanation: ^2 selects the second parent of a merge; ~n walks first parents.

questions.prompt: Run at 18:00, git log --since="2026-10-04" misses a commit made at 09:30 on 4 October. Why?
options: A date without a time uses the current time of day
questions.explanation: Git's date parser fills a missing time with the current time. Write --since="2026-10-04 00:00".

questions.prompt: Which command lists the commits on feature that main doesn't have?
questions.explanation: A..B selects commits reachable from B but not from A.

questions.prompt: What does a commit object store?
options: A diff against the parent and the branch name
A tree, parent ids, author, committer and message
The list of branches containing it
questions.explanation: A commit points to a full snapshot (tree) and its parents; branch names are separate refs.

interactions.title: Check yourself: branches, merges and conflicts

questions.prompt: During a merge you resolved the file and removed the markers. What marks it resolved?
questions.explanation: git add replaces the index's base/ours/theirs stages with your resolved version; then commit (or merge --continue).

questions.prompt: Which command returns the repository to its state before a conflicted merge started?
questions.explanation: git merge --abort reconstructs the pre-merge state.

questions.prompt: git branch -d feature/x says "not fully merged". What does that protect?
options: Commits that exist only on feature/x
questions.explanation: -d refuses when the branch has commits not merged into the current branch; -D would strand them (recoverable via the reflog for a while).

questions.prompt: A merge completes without conflicts. Is the result guaranteed to compile?
options: No — changes on different lines can still be incompatible
questions.explanation: Git merges text, not meaning. Build and test after every merge; CI on pull requests catches semantic conflicts.

interactions.title: Check yourself: rebasing and rewriting history

questions.prompt: During git rebase main, git checkout --theirs File.java keeps which version?
questions.explanation: In a rebase, ours is the new base (main plus replayed commits) and theirs is the commit being replayed — your work.

questions.prompt: After amending a pushed commit on your own PR branch, git status shows [ahead 1, behind 1]. What should you run?
questions.explanation: Pulling would merge the old commit back. Since the branch is yours, replace it with a lease that refuses if someone else pushed.

questions.prompt: Which commit should never be rewritten without team agreement?
options: A commit on your own PR branch nobody else uses
A commit on main that teammates have pulled
questions.explanation: Rewriting shared history leaves teammates with diverged copies; add a revert instead.

questions.prompt: In an interactive rebase, which command melds a commit into the one above it and discards its message?
questions.explanation: fixup combines and keeps only the previous message; squash lets you edit the combined message.

interactions.title: Check yourself: undoing and recovering work

questions.prompt: After an accidental git reset --hard HEAD~2 on a clean tree, how do you get the commits back?
questions.explanation: The reflog's HEAD@{1} is where HEAD was before the reset; resetting to it restores the branch.

questions.prompt: Which loss can the reflog NOT undo?
options: Unstaged edits overwritten by git restore
The pre-rebase version of a branch
questions.explanation: Unstaged edits were never stored as objects or commits, so nothing in Git remembers them.

questions.prompt: Which command undoes a commit that is already on the shared main branch?
questions.explanation: revert adds a new commit with the inverse change, so history isn't rewritten and everyone can pull normally.

questions.prompt: git stash pop reports a conflict. What happens to the stash entry?
options: It is kept until you drop it
It is converted into a commit
It is pushed to the remote
questions.explanation: pop drops the stash only if it applied cleanly; after a conflict it is kept.

questions.prompt: What does git fetch change?
questions.explanation: Fetch downloads objects and updates origin/*; it never moves your branches or touches your files.

questions.prompt: git push prints "! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)". What is the safe response?
options: Fetch, integrate (rebase or merge), test, then push
questions.explanation: The remote has commits you don't. Integrating them keeps your teammate's work; forcing would erase it.

questions.prompt: When does --force-with-lease refuse a push?
options: When the remote branch moved since your remote-tracking ref last saw it
When the branch has no upstream
questions.explanation: It replaces the branch only if it still points where origin/<branch> says. A background fetch can refresh that ref, so pin the expected commit when in doubt.

questions.prompt: Why aren't tags pushed by a plain git push?
options: Push sends the current branch by default; tags are pushed explicitly or with --follow-tags
questions.explanation: Push tags with git push origin v1.0.0 or --follow-tags (annotated tags on pushed commits).

interactions.title: Check yourself: GitHub, authentication and secrets

questions.prompt: A database password was pushed to a public repository. What comes first?
questions.explanation: The value may already be copied; only rotation makes it useless. Clean-up comes after.

questions.prompt: GitHub rejects your account password over HTTPS. What should you use?
options: A personal access token, browser sign-in or SSH
questions.explanation: Password authentication for Git operations was removed in 2021.

questions.prompt: Which file do you add to GitHub's SSH keys settings?
questions.explanation: Only the public key (.pub) is shared; the private key never leaves your machine.

questions.prompt: Fork vs clone — which statement is correct?
options: A fork is a server-side copy under your account; a clone is a local copy
questions.explanation: Forking is a GitHub feature used to contribute without write access; cloning is Git copying a repository locally.

interactions.title: Check yourself: pull requests and team workflows

questions.prompt: Why does git branch -d fail after a squash merge on GitHub?
options: Squash created a new commit; the branch's commits aren't ancestors of main
questions.explanation: Confirm the PR merged, then delete with -D.

questions.prompt: What reliably prevents unreviewed code reaching main?
options: Branch protection requiring PRs, approvals and status checks
questions.explanation: Only server-side rules apply to every push and merge; hooks can be skipped.

questions.prompt: Which workflow suits a team deploying several times a day?
questions.explanation: Frequent small integration into an always-releasable main fits continuous delivery; Gitflow suits scheduled, versioned releases.

questions.prompt: In a CODEOWNERS file, which line wins when several match?
options: The most specific path regardless of order
questions.explanation: Later lines override earlier ones, so put general rules first.

topics.after: Why Git Is Efficient at Snapshots

questions.prompt: Which object type stores a file's name?
questions.explanation: Trees list names, modes and object ids; blobs hold only contents.

questions.prompt: Two files with identical contents are committed. How many blobs are stored?
questions.explanation: Objects are content-addressed: same content, same id, stored once.

questions.prompt: Where is a branch stored?
options: As a ref: refs/heads/<name> (or a line in packed-refs) holding a commit id
questions.explanation: Branches are refs outside the object database; that's why they are cheap.

questions.prompt: What does git add do internally?
options: Writes a blob and updates the index entry
questions.explanation: The commit is built later from the index with write-tree and commit-tree.

interactions.title: Check yourself: search, bisect, hooks and specialised workflows

questions.prompt: Which command finds every commit that changed a line matching return .B. — including edits that keep the count the same?
questions.explanation: -S only reports changes in the number of occurrences; -G matches added or removed lines.

questions.prompt: In git bisect run, which exit code means "skip this commit"?
questions.explanation: 0 is good, 1–127 except 125 is bad, 125 skips, and codes above 127 abort.

questions.prompt: Why can't local hooks enforce team rules?
options: They aren't cloned automatically and can be skipped with --no-verify
questions.explanation: Enforcement belongs on the server: branch protection, required CI checks, push protection.

questions.prompt: You cloned a repository and libs/rubric is empty. What do you run?
questions.explanation: Submodules aren't checked out by a plain clone (use --recurse-submodules next time).

fetch updates origin/* only; pull = fetch + merge/rebase into the current branch.
merge adds a merge commit and keeps history; rebase replays commits on a new base with new ids (private branches only).
reset moves the branch back (rewrites); revert adds an undoing commit (safe on shared branches).
restore changes files and the index, never a branch; reset <commit> moves the branch.
checkout switches branches AND restores files; Git 2.23 split these into switch and restore.
Both re-apply; pop then drops the stash (only if there was no conflict).
clone = local copy (Git); fork = copy under your GitHub account (platform).
A tag is a Git ref copied with clones; a Release is GitHub data on a tag: notes, assets, flags.
--force overwrites unconditionally; the lease refuses if the remote moved since your last fetch.
Unstaged changes (working vs index) vs staged changes (index vs HEAD).
-S: commits changing the count of a string; -G: commits adding/removing lines matching a regex.
rm deletes the file and stages it; --cached untracks but keeps the file on disk.
The files on disk that you edit.
The proposed snapshot for the next commit.
What you have checked out — normally a pointer to the current branch.
HEAD points directly at a commit, not a branch; new commits belong to no branch.
origin/main: your local record of the remote branch at the last fetch, pull or push.
The remote branch a local branch tracks (git push -u sets it).
The best common ancestor of two branches; used by three-way merges and three-dot diffs.
Moving a branch pointer forward because the other branch already contains it — no merge commit.
A repository with no working tree, as used on servers.
Local log of where HEAD and branches pointed; used to recover lost commits.

Refuses to merge unless it can fast-forward.

One new commit for the whole PR; clean main; Git doesn't see the branch as merged.
Each PR commit re-created on top of the base; linear history; new commit ids.

Swapped: ours = the new base, theirs = your commit being replayed.
git reflog, then git reset --hard HEAD@{1} (or ORIG_HEAD).

cards.back: git branch <new>; git reset --hard HEAD~1; git switch <new>.
